observations.summary: The package contains a seeded tropical SpMV GPU benchmark with a CPU reference, numeric tolerance, median latency, and p99 latency.
The package contains repeated-run hash checks and records unresolved cross-device determinism differences.
The test setup can install mocks when live WebGPU initialization is unavailable, so a Doe harness must fail closed on provider identity.

reasons.summary: Doe can address an observed determinism problem while competing on an existing correctness-gated performance workload.
Doe receipts can make provider fallback and execution identity explicit.
The package owns GPU kernels, Node provider setup, correctness oracles, performance measurement, and determinism probes.
The reviewed harness confirmed that HoloScript's oracle-backed workload finds concrete Doe correctness defects and retains provider, execution, and output evidence for regression protection.
The separate upstream determinism probe remains a high-value next workload for Doe receipts and replay.
HoloScript continues to own GPU kernels, Node provider setup, correctness oracles, performance measurement, and determinism probes above the runtime provider boundary.

observations.summary: Gigi recursively executes a generated Node WebGPU test corpus and counts passing and failing cases.
A representative compute case initializes node-webgpu, captures validation errors, executes GPU work, and validates its output.
Gigi generates WebGPU and native rendering code, making it runtime- and compiler-adjacent rather than only a workload consumer.

reasons.summary: Doe can be evaluated across a broad, output-validating WebGPU corpus and can attach receipts to first failures.
Gigi already owns code generation, multi-target orchestration, execution tests, and output validation.
The reviewed provider-swap harness confirmed that Gigi's broad oracle-backed corpus can find and preserve concrete Doe compiler and runtime defects.
Gigi continues to own code generation, multi-target orchestration, execution tests, and output validation while depending on an external WebGPU runtime.

observations.summary: vgpu documents Node setup that supplies a WebGPU device to ONNX Runtime and then uses vgpu with zero-copy buffers.
vgpu compares deterministic RGBA output against committed PNG snapshots and emits actual and diff images on failure.

reasons.summary: Doe could supply the provider boundary for a realistic Node ML integration with an existing image oracle.
vgpu owns device orchestration, ML buffer integration, and deterministic output diagnostics above the provider boundary.

The reviewed provider-swap harness confirmed that vgpu's Node ORT integration can expose a deterministic Doe compatibility failure before inference and preserve the exact boundary for regression work.
vgpu owns device and GPU-buffer orchestration, numeric output validation, zero-copy identity checks, and lifecycle assertions while relying on an external WebGPU provider.

observations.summary: The project includes a CPU-versus-GPU SGD benchmark over multiple input sizes.
The benchmark constructs random inputs separately and does not verify the GPU embedding against a common output oracle.

A separate upstream WebGPU output suite uses deterministic cluster fixtures and validates finite output, embedding spread, topology preservation, nearest-neighbor labels, and controlled epoch scheduling.

reasons.summary: The project has a performance-sensitive GPU workload where Doe can compete once correctness and input identity are hardened.
The project owns a WebGPU algorithm and benchmark but not a general provider, runtime, or compiler layer.

The reviewed provider-swap harness confirms a realistic multi-epoch Doe compatibility workload, while physical-hardware performance and exact output identity remain valuable unresolved leverage points.
The project owns WebGPU SGD shaders, structural output oracles, and a benchmark but continues to rely on an external WebGPU provider and runtime.

observations.summary: The test setup can require live WebGPU and fail rather than silently skip when REQUIRE_WEBGPU is enabled.
The package documents real-device compile tests for several representative consumer shaders.
The upstream vegetation suite executes generated compute shaders and compares GPU records to an independent CPU oracle, including zero-candidate and overflow cases.
The upstream fullscreen suite executes generated vertex and fragment shaders, reads back RGBA8 output, and compares the first pixel to an independently calculated cosine-palette result.
The upstream consumer-device suite requires a deliberately invalid generated fragment shader to surface error-severity compilation information.

reasons.summary: Doe can provide compiler and initialization compatibility evidence for consumer shader workloads.
The package owns WebGPU provider setup and real-device compilation tests around its runtime integration.

The reviewed provider-swap harness exposes concrete Doe compiler, validation, and worker-lifecycle gaps across realistic generated compute and render workloads, while retaining independent upstream output oracles for regression proof.
The package owns WebGPU provider setup, dynamic shader generation, compute and render orchestration, readback, and execution oracles, but continues to rely on an external runtime implementation.

observations.summary: The test suite skips WebGPU compilation in CI to avoid native crashes.
The tests compile WGSL functions individually and together to detect compiler errors and symbol collisions.

The upstream compilation assertions decide shader validity solely from getCompilationInfo error messages, so a provider that logs native compiler failure without surfacing compilation messages can produce a false pass.

reasons.summary: Doe reliability and receipts directly target an observed native-crash boundary that prevents CI execution.
The package owns a shader corpus and compilation tests but not runtime-provider infrastructure.

The reviewed harness reproduces the pinned incumbent's native CI-class crash boundary while also showing that Doe can add value only after its compiler coverage and compilation-info reporting pass the strengthened corpus oracle.

The package owns a broad generated shader corpus, dependency resolution, and compilation assertions but not provider infrastructure, native compiler implementation, receipts, or execution diagnostics.

observations.summary: The project contains a machine-learning introduction whose WebGPU code is generated through Gigi.
The checked-in generated MNIST Node entrypoint imports the exact webgpu package specifier, providing a narrow provider-substitution seam without editing application or shader source.
The pinned generated workload includes its neural-network weights, ten image inputs, and six-pass WebGPU module, enabling a deterministic external CPU output oracle.

reasons.summary: The demo can validate Doe end to end on generated WebGPU ML code, although its evidence surface overlaps Gigi.
The project owns an application workload while delegating runtime-adjacent generation to Gigi.

The reviewed provider-swap workload exposes a reproducible Doe compiler and execution failure against an independent CPU oracle, while physical Vulkan correctness and performance remain unresolved leverage points.
The project owns the generated application graph, model assets, dispatch orchestration, and package seam while delegating code generation and runtime implementation to external components.

observations.summary: node-webgpu exposes Dawn's WebGPU implementation to Node and is the incumbent provider used by the downstream targets.

reasons.summary: The incumbent provider is primarily a comparison baseline rather than a likely Doe adopter.
node-webgpu implements the Node WebGPU provider boundary against which Doe is compared.

observations.summary: The package implements a Node-facing WebGPU runtime and therefore covers the same provider category as Doe.

reasons.summary: Doe receipts and cross-provider evidence may be useful, but this actor already owns its provider implementation.
The project implements the same Node WebGPU provider category as Doe.
